questions.question_text: The graph of $y = f(x)$ has an $x$-intercept at $(7, 0)$ and a $y$-intercept at $(0, -14)$. Which line is a vertical asymptote of $y = \dfrac{1}{f(x)}$?

options.why: Used the y-intercept value instead of the zero of the function.
Confused a vertical asymptote equation x = k with a horizontal line equation.
Reciprocated the x-coordinate instead of taking the zero where f(x) = 0.

questions.solution_text:
A vertical asymptote of $y = \dfrac{1}{f(x)}$ occurs where $f(x) = 0$.
Since the $x$-intercept is $(7, 0)$, $f(7) = 0$.
Therefore the vertical asymptote is $x = 7$.

questions.question_text: The function $y = f(x) = 8 - x$ is a linear function. Find the coordinates of the invariant points where the curves $y = f(x)$ and $y = \dfrac{1}{f(x)}$ intersect.

options.why: Solved $8 - x = 1$ by adding $1$ to $8$ instead of subtracting, giving $x = 9$.
Solved $8 - x = -1$ by subtracting $1$ from $8$ instead of adding, giving $x = 7$.
Made the sign slip in both equations, adding where subtraction was needed and subtracting where addition was needed.

questions.solution_text:
Invariant points occur where $f(x) = 1$ and $f(x) = -1$:
$8 - x = 1 \implies x = 7$, giving $(7, 1)$
$8 - x = -1 \implies x = 9$, giving $(9, -1)$
Invariant points are $(7, 1)$ and $(9, -1)$.

questions.question_text: The quadratic $f(x) = (x - 5)(x + 7)$ has zeros at $x = 5$ and $x = -7$. In which interval is the reciprocal function $y = \dfrac{1}{f(x)}$ strictly negative?

options.why: Selected the regions where the parabola is positive rather than negative.
Inverted the signs of the roots of the quadratic function.
Selected only one unbounded positive region instead of the negative interval.

questions.solution_text:
The parabola $f(x) = x^2 + 2x - 35$ opens upwards with zeros at $x = -7$ and $x = 5$.
Between the zeros, for $-7 < x < 5$, $f(x) < 0$.
Since $\dfrac{1}{f(x)}$ has the same sign as $f(x)$, $y < 0$ for $-7 < x < 5$.

questions.question_text: The curve $y = f(x)$ has a local minimum at $(4, -8)$. Determine the coordinates and nature of the corresponding turning point on $y = \dfrac{1}{f(x)}$.

options.why: Inverted the y-value but failed to invert the nature from minimum to maximum.
Negated the x-coordinate and incorrectly made the y-coordinate positive.
Reciprocated the x-coordinate as well as the y-coordinate.

questions.solution_text:
The $x$-coordinate remains $x = 4$.
The $y$-coordinate is the reciprocal: $y = \dfrac{1}{-8} = -\dfrac{1}{8}$.
A local minimum with negative value becomes a local maximum.
Local maximum at $\left(4, -\dfrac{1}{8}\right)$.

questions.question_text: A function $y = f(x)$ is positive for all real $x$ and has range $[3, \infty)$. What is the range of the reciprocal function $y = \dfrac{1}{f(x)}$?

options.why: Inverted the minimum value without reversing the inequality direction.
Kept the upper bound 3 without reciprocating it.
Introduced negative values when the original function is strictly positive.

questions.solution_text:
Since $f(x) \ge 3$ for all $x$:
$\dfrac{1}{f(x)} \le \dfrac{1}{3}$
Since $f(x) > 0$, $\dfrac{1}{f(x)} > 0$.
As $f(x) \to \infty$, $\dfrac{1}{f(x)} \to 0^+$.
Range is $\left(0, \dfrac{1}{3}\right]$.

questions.question_text: The curve $y = f(x)$ has a horizontal asymptote at $y = -6$. What is the horizontal asymptote of $y = \dfrac{1}{f(x)}$?

options.why: Assumed all reciprocal functions have horizontal asymptote y = 0.
Negated the asymptote value instead of reciprocating it.
Confused a horizontal asymptote equation with a vertical line equation.

questions.question_text: The function $f(x) = x^2 - 10x + 24$ has vertex $(5, -1)$ and zeros at $x = 4$ and $x = 6$. What is the range of $y = \dfrac{1}{f(x)}$?

options.why: Inverted the interval [-1, 0) incorrectly into [-1, 0).
Omitted the positive branch corresponding to x < 4 and x > 6.
Ignored the excluded band between y = -1 and y = 0.

questions.solution_text:
On the interval $(4, 6)$, $f(x)$ takes values in $[-1, 0)$, so $\dfrac{1}{f(x)}$ takes values in $(-\infty, -1]$.
On $(-\infty, 4) \cup (6, \infty)$, $f(x)$ takes values in $(0, \infty)$, so $\dfrac{1}{f(x)}$ takes values in $(0, \infty)$.
Combining these gives the range $(-\infty, -1] \cup (0, \infty)$.

questions.question_text: The function $f(x) = \dfrac{x + 5}{x - 7}$ has a vertical asymptote at $x = 7$ and zero at $x = -5$. Which statement correctly describes the graph of $g(x) = \dfrac{1}{f(x)}$?

options.text: Vertical asymptote at $x = -5$, zero at $x = 7$, and horizontal asymptote at $y = 1$
Vertical asymptote at $x = 7$, zero at $x = -5$, and horizontal asymptote at $y = 1$
options.why: Described the original function f(x) instead of its reciprocal g(x).

options.text: Vertical asymptote at $x = -5$, vertical asymptote at $x = 7$, and horizontal asymptote at $y = 0$
options.why: Treated the original vertical asymptote as a remaining vertical asymptote.

options.text: Vertical asymptote at $x = -5$, zero at $x = 7$, and horizontal asymptote at $y = -1$
options.why: Incorrectly negated the horizontal asymptote value.

questions.solution_text:
$g(x) = \dfrac{x - 7}{x + 5}$.
Vertical asymptote occurs where $x + 5 = 0 \implies x = -5$.
Zero of $g(x)$ is at $x = 7$.
Horizontal asymptote: $\lim_{x \to \pm\infty} \dfrac{x - 7}{x + 5} = 1$, so $y = 1$.
